This Bills Digest replaces a preliminary Digest published on 29 May 2026 to assist in early consideration of the Bill.

## Key points

- The [Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query%3DId%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7493%22) (the Bill) and the [Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7492%22) (the Imposition Bill) are the first tranche of proposed legislation to implement part of the Government’s 2026–27 Budget tax reforms. The Bills passed the House of Representatives on 4 June 2026.
- The Bills will:
  - replace the 50% Capital Gains Tax (CGT) discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax rate on capital gains accruing from 1 July 2027 ( **Schedule 1** to the Bill and the **Imposition Bill**)
  - limit negative gearing for residential property investments to new builds from 1 July 2027 ( **Schedule 2**)
  - introduce the Working Australians Tax Offset, a non-refundable tax offset for Australian resident individuals who earn labour income ( **Schedule 3**)
  - introduce a $1,000 standard deduction for work-related expenses for individuals who are Australian tax residents who derive assessable labour income ( **Schedule 4**).
- The proposed changes to CGT and negative gearing are the most controversial elements of the Bills and have attracted considerable stakeholder comment. The Government continues to consult with key stakeholders on these issues.
- The Bills have been referred to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee for [inquiry and report](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Senate/Economics/TLABITRTaxReform) by 22 June 2026. At the time of writing, the Committee had received [167 submissions](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Senate/Economics/TLABITRTaxReform/Submissions).

Introductory Info **Date of introduction:** 28 May 2026

**House introduced in:** House of Representatives

**Portfolio:** Treasury

**Commencement:** Parts 1, 3 and 4 of Schedule 1 and Schedules 3 and 4 to the [Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query%3DId%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7493%22) (Bill) and the [Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7492%22) (Imposition Bill), commence on the first 1 January, 1 April, 1 July or 1 October occurring after Royal Assent.

Part 2 of Schedule 1 to the Bill commences at the same time as the Imposition Bill, but only if the Imposition Bill commences.

Schedule 2 to the Bill commences on the day after Royal Assent.

## Purpose and structure of the Bills

The [Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query%3DId%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7493%22) (the Bill) amends taxation legislation to:

- replace the 50% Capital Gains Tax (CGT) discount for individuals, trusts and partnerships with cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax rate on capital gains accruing from 1 July 2027 ( **Schedule 1**)
- limit negative gearing for residential property investments to new builds from 1 July 2027 ( **Schedule 2**)
- introduce the Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO), a non-refundable tax offset for Australian resident individuals who earn labour income ( **Schedule 3**)
- introduce a $1,000 standard deduction for work-related expenses for individuals who are Australian tax residents who derive assessable labour income ( **Schedule 4**).

The [Income Tax Rates Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Bill 2026](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr7492%22) (the Imposition Bill) amends the [Income Tax Rates Act 1986](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A03348/latest/text) (ITRA) to impose a minimum 30% tax on capital gains that are realised on or after 1 July 2027. The tax is imposed in a separate Bill to comply with constitutional requirements.

## Schedules 1 and 2: Reforming negative gearing and CGT

### The rationale for, and origins of, the CGT and the 50% CGT discount

Before 1985, Australia had no general tax on capital gains. In 1975, the [Asprey Taxation Review Committee](https://treasury.gov.au/publication/economic-roundup-winter-2006/a-brief-history-of-australias-tax-system#:~:text=Taxation%20Review%20Committee%20in%20the%20early%201970s%20(Asprey%20et%20al%201975).#:~:text=Taxation%20Review%20Committee%20in%20the%20early%201970s%20(Asprey%20et%20al%201975).) was the first to [recommend a CGT](https://dpslibrary.softlinkhosting.com.au/liberty/OpacLogin?mode=BASIC&openDetail=true&corporation=DPSLibrary&action=search&queryTerm=uuid%3D%22a733f2d20a5a015560b81aa20000c50b%22&editionUuid=a733f2d20a5a015560b81aa20000c50b&operator=OR&url=%2Fopac%2Fsearch.do), noting that the absence of a CGT encouraged investment in assets delivering capital appreciation rather than income, thereby distorting economic decision‑making (p. 18, paragraph 3.36). Although initially considered by the [Whitlam Government](https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/aph/reader.action?docID=6512771&c=UERG&ppg=310), the proposal was not pursued (p. 289).

The 1985 [Reform of the Australian Taxation System: Draft White Paper](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query%3DId%3A%E2%80%9Dlibrary%2Fjrnart%2FT9MO6%E2%80%9D)recommended the introduction of a CGT (p. 255, paragraph 22.56). The paper further observed that the absence of a CGT facilitated tax avoidance, particularly through arrangements converting income into tax-free capital gains (pp. 77–78). On that basis, the Hawke-Keating Government [quickly introduced](https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/aph/reader.action?docID=6512771&c=UERG&ppg=310) a prospective CGT regime in former Part IIIA of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 (ITAA36), applying to an asset acquired and disposed of on or after 20 September 1985 (p. 290).

However, the original CGT provisions (1985–1998) proved problematic. They were widely [criticised](https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/aph/reader.action?docID=6512771&c=UERG&ppg=311) for being overly complex, unfair, and distortive of commercial decisions (p. 290).

The [Tax Law Improvement Project](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22library%2Fprspub%2FSH530%22) (1993–1997) [re-wrote the CGT regime](https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/aph/reader.action?docID=6512771&c=UERG&ppg=312) to be based on the identification of a series of CGT events that can arise in a variety of situations, (for example, sale of shares or an investment property, or purchase of land) (pp. 290–291). The rewritten CGT provisions, effective from 1 July 1998, are contained in Parts 3-1 and 3-3 of the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1997](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A05138/latest/text) (ITAA97) (p. 291).

In 1999, the Howard Government made significant CGT reforms following the [Ralph Review of Business Taxation](https://dpslibrary.softlinkhosting.com.au/liberty/OpacLogin?mode=BASIC&openDetail=true&corporation=DPSLibrary&action=search&queryTerm=uuid%3D%22a75e9c8f0a5a015541d7c623002157c9%22&editionUuid=a75e9c8f0a5a015541d7c623002157c9&operator=OR&url=%2Fopac%2Fsearch.do). These [included](https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/aph/reader.action?c=UERG&docID=6512771&ppg=312) the introduction of a 50% CGT discount for individuals and certain trusts where assets are held for at least 12 months, the freezing of indexation after 21 September 1999 and the extension of the small business CGT concessions (p. 291).

### Overview of current CGT and negative gearing

[**Key design features**](https://ebookcentral.proquest.com/lib/aph/reader.action?docID=6512771&c=UERG&ppg=312) of the current CGT regime include (pp. 291–292):

- A capital gain arises where the capital proceeds from the CGT event exceed the asset costs ( [section 100-35](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s100.35.html)). Net capital gains are ‘fed back’, or included, in the taxpayer’s assessable income ( [section 102-5(1)](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s102.5.html)).
- Assets acquired before 20 September 1985 ( **pre-CGT assets**) are currently [exempt from CGT](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/list-of-cgt-assets-and-exemptions#ato-Assetsacquiredbefore20September1985:~:text=a%20CGT%20exemption-,Assets%20acquired%20before%2020%20September%201985,a%20result%20of%20the%20sale%20of%20a%20pre%2DCGT%20asset.,-Real%20estate). This ‘grandfathering’ of pre-CGT assets is unique to the Australian CGT. All other countries that have introduced a CGT have taxed the gains that arise after the date of introduction of the tax, regardless of whether the asset was acquired before or after that date.
- **Pre-21 September 1999:** CGT was only imposed on ‘real gains’, meaning that [an asset’s cost was adjusted by the rate of inflation](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/indexing-the-cost-base#:~:text=The%20indexation%20method%20adjusts%20the%20amount%20of%20an%20asset%27s%20costs%20by%20the%20rate%20of%20inflation.%20The%20adjustment%20is%20based%20on%20the%20consumer%20price%20index%20(CPI).#:~:text=The%20indexation%20method%20adjusts%20the%20amount%20of%20an%20asset%27s%20costs%20by%20the%20rate%20of%20inflation.%20The%20adjustment%20is%20based%20on%20the%20consumer%20price%20index%20(CPI).), based on the consumer price index (CPI). The increased cost amounts reduced the capital gain on the asset. The indexation factor was determined quarterly. (Capital losses, however, were never indexed.) The ATO provides [an example](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/calculating-your-cgt/indexing-the-cost-base#:~:text=Example%3A%20indexing%20the,to%20calculate%20CGT.#:~:text=Example%3A%20indexing%20the,to%20calculate%20CGT.) on how to index a cost base.
- **On and after 21 September 1999**: a [CGT discount](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount) of 50% is available in respect of disposals by an Australian resident individual or trust where the asset has been held for more than 12 months. The eligible taxpayer can apply the 50% CGT discount by excluding 50% of the capital gain that arises from a CGT event from their assessable income ( [section 115-100](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s115.100.html) ITAA97). A complying superannuation fund is entitled to a one-third discount.
- Capital losses are ‘quarantined’, meaning that they can only be offset against capital gains (though they may be carried forward indefinitely for offset). They are not allowed as a deduction from assessable income.
- For resident individuals, net capital gains are taxed at marginal rates in the year of income of the CGT event. CGT is charged on resident taxpayers in respect of all CGT events, no matter where assets involved in the CGT event may be located.

#### Negative gearing

‘ [Negative gearing](https://treasury.gov.au/review/tax-white-paper/negative-gearing#:~:text=You%20won%E2%80%99t%20find,in%20producing%20income.#:~:text=You%20won%E2%80%99t%20find,in%20producing%20income.)’ describes a situation where expenses (including interest expenses) associated with an asset exceed the income earned from the asset. It is not defined in tax legislation. Negative gearing can apply to any type of investment, not just housing.

Individuals who are [negatively geared](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/property-and-land/residential-rental-properties/rental-expenses/how-to-claim-rental-expenses#ato-Positiveornegativegearing:~:text=negatively%20geared%20if,capital%20gains%20tax.#ato-Positiveornegativegearing:~:text=negatively%20geared%20if,capital%20gains%20tax.) can deduct their loss against other income, such as salary, wages or business income. If the other income is not enough to absorb the loss, the loss can be carried forward to the next income year.

Australia’s tax system currently operates on the principle that people pay tax on their personal income less any deductible expenses in generating that income.

### Inquiries and calls for reform

Amid a worsening housing crisis, calls for tax reforms have intensified. The [Australian Greens](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F8093625%22), [Allegra Spender](https://theconversation.com/politics-with-michelle-grattan-independent-mp-allegra-spender-on-making-tax-fairer-for-younger-australians-262225), [Senator David Pocock](https://www.davidpocock.com.au/housing_2025#:~:text=Advocacy%20on%20housing%20tax%20reform%C2%A0) and former Treasury Secretary [Dr Ken Henry](https://theconversation.com/politics-with-michelle-grattan-treasury-veteran-ken-henry-on-the-enormous-damage-the-tax-system-does-to-young-people-259887), among others, have raised intergenerational inequity concerns about the tax system. Notably, Allegra Spender [released](https://www.allegraspender.com.au/tax) a [Tax Green Paper](https://apo.org.au/node/329119) (November 2024) and a [Tax White Paper](https://www.allegraspender.com.au/tax#:~:text=Tax%20White%20Paper%20%2D%20What%20I%27m%20proposing) (March 2026).

In August 2025, a 3-day [Economic Reform Roundtable](https://treasury.gov.au/review/economic-reform-roundtable), led by the Treasurer, was held with the aim of building consensus on improving productivity, enhancing economic resilience and strengthening budget sustainability. [Day 3](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-10/foi-4025.pdf) focused on tax reform.

In November 2025, the [Select Committee on the Operation of the Capital Gains Tax Discount](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Senate/Operation_of_the_Capital_Gains_Tax_Discount#:~:text=On%204%20November%202025%2C%20the%20Senate%20resolved%20that%20the%20Select%20Committee%20on%20the%20Operation%20of%20the%20Capital%20Gains%20Tax%20Discount%C2%A0be%20established.#:~:text=On%204%20November%202025%2C%20the%20Senate%20resolved%20that%20the%20Select%20Committee%20on%20the%20Operation%20of%20the%20Capital%20Gains%20Tax%20Discount%C2%A0be%20established.) was established, chaired by Australian Greens Senator Nick McKim and comprising 2 Labor senators, 2 Liberal senators and independent Senator David Pocock. The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) [provided costing advice](https://www.pbo.gov.au/publications-and-data/publications/costings/operation-CGT-discount) to the Committee in February 2026. The Committee’s [final report](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Senate/Operation_of_the_Capital_Gains_Tax_Discount/CapitalGainsTaxDiscount/Report) (released on 17 March 2026) found evidence that (p. vii):

- Amongst other factors, the combination of the CGT discount and negative gearing has skewed housing ownership away from owner-occupiers and towards investors (Finding 3). This could potentially distort decision-making and incentivise tax planning (Finding 1).
- The CGT discount potentially distorts the allocation of investment across the economy, with evidence that existing housing stock makes up a substantial share of capital gains that benefit from the capital gains tax discount (Finding 2).
- The benefits of the CGT discount are unequally distributed, with implications for income and wealth inequality and intergenerational inequality (Finding 4).

The Coalition senators dissented and criticised the Chair's report as a ‘simplistic and one‑dimensional analysis of Australian housing policy’ (p. 111). They advised that the Coalition believes that the current CGT discount was working as intended and should not be changed (p. 111).

The Greens called for the CGT discount to be abolished for investment properties and substantially reined in across all asset classes, along with broader tax reform (pp. 106–108).

The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet released a [Treasury Supplementary Analysis](https://oia.pmc.gov.au/sites/default/files/posts/2026/05/Supplementary%20Analysis_1.pdf)in May 2026.

### Budget 2026–27 and the Bills

In his second reading speech on the Bills, the Treasurer Dr Jim Chalmers [flagged consultation](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22chamber%2Fhansardr%2F29160%2F0020%22#:~:text=As%20outlined%20in,legislation%20following%20consultation.#:~:text=As%20outlined%20in,legislation%20following%20consultation.) on the CGT treatment of small and start-up businesses and further consideration of interactions with ‘attribution managed investment trusts, tax consolidation, residency changes’ and ‘other relevant issues’. He mentioned that ‘details will be finalised in subsequent legislation following consultation’, where appropriate. The Treasurer further [stated](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22chamber%2Fhansardr%2F29160%2F0020%22#:~:text=Firstly%2C%20we%20are,are%20the%20facts.#:~:text=Firstly%2C%20we%20are,are%20the%20facts.):

> Firstly, we are not introducing a tax on inheritances or inherited assets. Secondly, people will still have their capital gains tax reduced under the new system, with the reduction now accurately reflecting inflation. Thirdly, the vast majority of small businesses in this country will remain eligible for generous CGT concessions. This means the overwhelming majority of small businesses can pay reduced or no capital gains tax when they sell. These are the facts.

On 25 May 2026, the Prime Minister [announced](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F10865416%22) a staged legislative approach to introducing the changes announced in the Budget:

- the first tranche, comprising proposed framework legislation (i.e. the current Bills) was introduced on 28 May 2026
- following consultation, a second tranche of proposed legislation to implement the detailed measures will be introduced (p. 3).

#### CGT reforms ([Budget Measures: Budget Paper No. 2: 2026–27](https://budget.gov.au/content/bp2/download/bp2_2026-27.pdf), pp. 21–22).

- From 1 July 2027, the 50% CGT discount will be replaced by cost base indexation for assets held for more than 12 months, and a 30% minimum tax on net capital gains. These changes will apply to all CGT assets, including pre-1985 CGT assets, held by individuals, trusts and partnerships.
- The Government states that the new 30% minimum tax is intended to reduce incentives to defer capital gains realisations to low marginal tax rates years (for example, retirement) and to ensure gains are taxed at rates more consistent with those applying during taxpayers’ working lives ( [Budget 2026–27 Tax Explainer](https://budget.gov.au/content/factsheets/download/tax-explainers-negative-gearing-capital-gains-tax.pdf), p. 2).
- **Transitional rules**: CGT changes only apply to gains arising on or after 1 July 2027. The 50% CGT discount will continue to apply to gains arising before 1 July 2027. Capital gains on pre-1985 assets arising before 1 July 2027 will remain exempt from CGT.
- **New builds:** Investors in new residential properties will be able to choose either the 50% CGT discount, or cost base indexation and the minimum tax.
- **Age pensioners exempted:** Income support payment recipients, including Age Pension recipients, will be exempt from the minimum tax.

#### Negative gearing reforms

- From 1 July 2027, negative gearing for residential property will be limited to new builds.
- Losses from established residential properties:
  - will only be deductible against rental income or the capital gains from residential properties
  - can be carried forward and offset against residential property income in future years.
- Grandfathering applies to properties acquired before 7:30PM (AEST) on 12 May 2026 (including contracts entered into but not yet settled).
- [Exemptions](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe22635b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?navigationPath=Search%2Fv1%2Fresults%2Fnavigation%2Fi0a93c4750000019ea9d53e98b89c854f%3Fppcid%3Dbcdce661999c458d9d7963751d9b519d%26Nav%3DAUNZ_CURRENT_AWARENESS%26fragmentIdentifier%3DI47fe22635b2911f184d0de003bc213a9%26parentRank%3D0%26startIndex%3D1%26contextData%3D%2528sc.Search%2529%26transitionType%3DSearchItem&listSource=Search&listPageSource=1d96f857d2041138e8cae306bbcc223d&list=AUNZ_CURRENT_AWARENESS&rank=4&sessionScopeId=fa317c515a8588edc0d0953725f747b982521f28a045032b88efd39349d1d095&ppcid=bcdce661999c458d9d7963751d9b519d&originationContext=Search%20Result&transitionType=SearchItem&contextData=(sc.Search)&comp=wlau#:~:text=Exclusions,providing%20fringe%20benefits.#:~:text=Exclusions,providing%20fringe%20benefits.)from the negative gearing changes are available for:

  - eligible new builds (to increase housing stock)
  - properties held by widely held trusts and superannuation funds
  - targeted build-to-rent developments and private investors supporting government housing programs.

The Treasurer [indicated](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/transcripts/interview-david-speers-insiders-abc-12#:~:text=over%20the%2010%E2%80%91year%20period%2C%20the%20capital%20gains%20and%20negative%20gearing%20changes%20are%20a%20little%20bit%20over%20%2440%C2%A0billion) that the reforms to CGT changes and negative gearing were expected to raise just over $40 billion over 10 years. The Government also advised that the OECD had recommended reducing or eliminating the CGT discount and phasing out negative gearing to improve Australia’s tax system ( [Tax Explainer](https://budget.gov.au/content/factsheets/download/tax-explainers-negative-gearing-capital-gains-tax.pdf), p. 5; [OECD Economic Surveys: Australia](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-australia-2026_d22a1efd-en.html), pp. 39–40).

#### Concessions retained — small business, main residence

The existing [4 small business CGT concessions](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/incentives-and-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions) remain [unchanged](https://budget.gov.au/content/factsheets/download/tax-explainers-negative-gearing-capital-gains-tax.pdf) (p. 4).

Small businesses with aggregated annual turnover [below $2 million](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/incentives-and-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions-eligibility-conditions/cgt-small-business-entity-eligibility#:~:text=aggregated%20turnover%20of-,less%20than%20%242%20million.,-Aggregated%20turnover%20is) or net assets [less than $6 million](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/incentives-and-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions-eligibility-conditions/maximum-net-asset-value-test#:~:text=To%20meet%20the%20test%2C%20the%20total%20net%20value%20of%20CGT%20assets%20owned%20by%20you%2C%20entities%20connected%20with%20you%2C%20affiliates%20and%20entities%20connected%20with%20your%20affiliates%2C%20must%20not%20exceed%20%246%C2%A0million.#:~:text=To%20meet%20the%20test%2C%20the%20total%20net%20value%20of%20CGT%20assets%20owned%20by%20you%2C%20entities%20connected%20with%20you%2C%20affiliates%20and%20entities%20connected%20with%20your%20affiliates%2C%20must%20not%20exceed%20%246%C2%A0million.), will [remain eligible for substantial discounts on capital gains](https://www.afr.com/policy/tax-and-super/investors-dispute-treasury-s-cgt-analysis-20260519-p5zyme#:~:text=Small%20businesses%20with%20revenue%20below%20%242%20million%2C%20superannuation%20funds%20and%20foreign%20investors%20will%20remain%20eligible%20for%20significant%20discounts%20on%20capital%20gains%2C%20despite%20the%20introduction%20of%20a%20minimum%2030%20per%20cent%20rate%20on%20real%20gains%20earned%20by%20locals.#:~:text=Small%20businesses%20with%20revenue%20below%20%242%20million%2C%20superannuation%20funds%20and%20foreign%20investors%20will%20remain%20eligible%20for%20significant%20discounts%20on%20capital%20gains%2C%20despite%20the%20introduction%20of%20a%20minimum%2030%20per%20cent%20rate%20on%20real%20gains%20earned%20by%20locals.).

The [main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence---home/eligibility-for-main-residence-exemption) remains CGT exempt. The [existing 60% CGT discount for eligible affordable housing](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/property-and-land/residential-rental-properties/rental-affordability-schemes/investing-in-affordable-rental-housing) is retained ( [Tax Explainer](https://budget.gov.au/content/factsheets/download/tax-explainers-negative-gearing-capital-gains-tax.pdf), p. 4).

#### State governments

### Reactions to the Budget and the Bills

#### Strong backlash

The CGT changes attracted strong reactions, amplified by a [social media meme](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-05-22/one-nation-wave-albanese-labor-chalmers-budget-backlash/106692278). On [Insiders](https://aus01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Femms.aph.gov.au%2Fparliament%2Fdetails%2F6459914%2Fprogram&data=05%7C02%7CElo.Guo-Hawkins%40aph.gov.au%7Cb450e1eb407c4c691d2608deba9def3e%7Cf6214c153a9947d1b862c9648e927316%7C0%7C0%7C639153384779162698%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=N%2BN3jtWCjWbTbyh0Hpg55MZjGWsu0jD5gwKK0KPs2%2FA%3D&reserved=0) (from 09:02:38) David Speers noted a ‘flood of complaints’ (particularly from [entrepreneurs and business owners](https://www.afr.com/technology/albanese-mocked-by-entrepreneurs-using-ai-images-to-fight-cgt-changes-20260518-p5zy6a)) over the idea all investments would be hit with new capital gains tax rules. Michelle Grattan observed that the response had been dramatic and [not in the way the Government expected](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-05-22/one-nation-wave-albanese-labor-chalmers-budget-backlash/106692278#:~:text=But%20they%20underestimated%20the%20extent%20and%20ferocity%20of%20the%20backlash%2C%20which%20has%20gone%20not%20only%20to%20broken%20promises%20but%20deep%20into%20the%20weeds%20of%20individual%20measures%2C%20notably%20relating%20to%20CGT%20and%20trusts.#:~:text=But%20they%20underestimated%20the%20extent%20and%20ferocity%20of%20the%20backlash%2C%20which%20has%20gone%20not%20only%20to%20broken%20promises%20but%20deep%20into%20the%20weeds%20of%20individual%20measures%2C%20notably%20relating%20to%20CGT%20and%20trusts.), especially the extent and ferocity of the backlash and the ‘loud voice’ from some critical younger people. Alicia Barry, Finance Reporter from ABC News, [mentioned](https://www.youtube.com/live/OtAOBcDPQiI) that there had been a ‘big misinformation campaign’ which claimed small businesses that are carved out of the measures are subject to hefty CGTs (from 1:10:47 to 1:13:49).

#### Support for CGT and negative gearing reforms

[Paul Keating](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/may/21/keating-lashes-coalition-startup-sector-claims-cgt-capital-gains-tax-tech-startups-canva) argued that the reforms address long‑standing distortions favouring capital over labour and housing over other investment, and that wealthy individuals had benefited from these tax system ‘distortions’ for decades. He described the CGT and negative gearing changes as ‘marginal’ and ‘badly needed’ to improve housing affordability. He also contended that the 50% CGT discount introduced by the Howard Government dramatically fuelled house prices in Australia.

[Graeme Samuel](https://theconversation.com/politics-with-michelle-grattan-graeme-samuel-on-doomsday-attacks-on-the-federal-budget-284430) said the tax reforms ‘ [are actually quite mild](https://theconversation.com/politics-with-michelle-grattan-graeme-samuel-on-doomsday-attacks-on-the-federal-budget-284430#:~:text=are%20actually%20quite%20mild)’ and pointed to economist [Saul Eslake](https://johnmenadue.com/post/2026/05/some-further-thoughts-on-the-tax-changes-in-the-2026-27-federal-budget/#:~:text=why%20should%20someone,of%20investment%20income%3F) as best explaining the Budget’s key issue, which he perceived as:

> why should people earning the same income in different ways be treated differently by the income tax system?… why should someone who earns, say, $100,000 in the form of wages and salaries – or, for that matter, interest – be expected to contribute more to the cost of providing teachers, doctors and nurses, police officers, and the broad range of services governments are expected to provide, than someone who earns $100,000 from capital gains, operating a business, trust distributions or other types of investment income?

[Robert Breunig](https://www.afr.com/politics/federal/australia-s-most-ambitious-tax-reform-in-decades-deserves-support-20260512-p5zw5d) credited the Government for ‘taking on the poisonous job of tax reform’. He considered that the negative gearing and CGT reform contributed ‘significantly towards unwinding distortions’ and that the ‘CGT reform will deter some activity around starting and selling businesses but simultaneously reduce the tax-fuelled appeal of property investment.’ The [Grattan Institute](https://theconversation.com/rising-rents-and-death-taxes-why-wild-claims-after-the-budget-dont-actually-make-sense-283283#:~:text=Putting%20tax%20reform%20in%20the%20%E2%80%98too%20hard%20basket%E2%80%99%20hurts%20us%20all) argued that ‘putting tax reform in the “too hard basket” hurts us all’.

The [Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA)](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880709/upload_binary/10880709.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880709%22), the [Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU)](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880704/upload_binary/10880704.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880704%22), [Urban Taskforce Australia](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880778/upload_binary/10880778.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880778%22), and [ACOSS, Everybody’s Home, Better Renting and National Shelter](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880702/upload_binary/10880702.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880702%22) broadly supported the reforms, describing them as a positive – albeit overdue – step towards improving housing affordability, while calling for swift passage of the Bills. [Urban Taskforce Australia](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880778/upload_binary/10880778.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880778%22) also called for an additional $15.6 billion housing-related infrastructure funding over 3 years.

The [Australian Finance Industry Association (AFIA)](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880706/upload_binary/10880706.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880706%22) supported the reforms alongside complementary supply-side measures ($2 billion local infrastructure fund), but emphasised the need for ‘broader supply-side reform to address painful planning and infrastructure shortfalls,’ and cautioned against undermining investor confidence. [Oxfam Australia](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880757/upload_binary/10880757.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880757%22) welcomed the changes as ‘modest’ and called for bolder action to tackle inequality by taxing the super-rich (p. 2).

#### Opposition to the tax reforms

Business groups, including the [Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry](https://acci.com.au/Web/News/Articles/2026/Business-chambers-urge-government-to-scrap-business-tax-hikes.aspx) (ACCI) and state and territory chambers, urged the Government to ‘rethink’ the CGT and trust changes, and stop the ‘damaging business tax hikes’. The ACCI said that the business community was shocked by the new taxes on business, and argued that the reforms lacked an economic rationale. Some polling cited by [The Fair Go](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880731/upload_binary/10880731.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880731%22) suggested limited public support and signs of reduced investment intentions.

Property and housing stakeholders, particularly the [Real Estate Institute of Australia (REIA)](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880764/upload_binary/10880764.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880764%22), warned the reforms could risk undermining housing delivery at a critical time, as modelling indicated around 25,500 fewer homes would be built over the next 5 years. REIA argued that improving affordability required increased housing supply rather than changes to tax settings.

Tech companies, start-ups, early-stage venture capitalist stakeholders and related recruitment firms, such as the [Tech Council of Australia](https://youtu.be/ykD_N6ZyiP0?si=loZTrGabUl4FwlnN), [Oktopi](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=abfa84ef-25c7-46f4-8e00-37cb0ab1fd62&subId=791868), [Tier One People](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=893eca1e-35df-4337-926b-5be0abda20f7&subId=792192), [Otso Capital](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=df9254f9-c6ba-4c50-8a94-3c9daf39b89d&subId=792454) and [Defender Ventures](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=c99f4743-96f3-49e6-adf9-d762ac79c6cf&subId=793061), contended the reforms could discourage risk‑taking, reduce competitiveness, and prompt capital and talent to move offshore. The [Tech Council](https://youtu.be/ykD_N6ZyiP0?si=loZTrGabUl4FwlnN) argued the broader CGT changes could potentially double the tax where the cost base is $0, and weaken Australia’s high-risk, high‑reward tech ecosystem (with an estimated 5% success rate) for many years; and mentioned that the absence of a clear legislative definition of a ‘startup’ was also an issue which was being addressed with the Government.

Small business submitters ( [Storage Lord](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=e41b246e-4fdc-4944-9dd1-dc6d5450287b&subId=793232) and [Deegan and Co](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=8a8b3ae1-8161-4342-94c6-736f5b52d35f&subId=793281)) argued that small businesses should be carved out of the measures as the reform would hurt the return on sales of small business that have been built over a long period, with the 30% minimum tax punishing the wrong people; and create unintended consequences for share investors, junior miners and explorers, and distortions in the superannuation sector.

[Professor David Stern](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=611b790d-6c26-433c-9a42-49e2c7791f6d&subId=792419) argued that the changes disincentivised the risk-taking, innovation, and investment that help drive productivity growth.

#### Economic and market impacts

The [Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA](https://www.afr.com/policy/economy/tax-changes-and-rate-rises-risk-cooling-housing-rba-says-20260517-p5zxvw?btis#:~:text=Reserve%20Bank%20of%20Australia%20assistant%20governor%20Sarah%20Hunter%20has%20said%20risks%20cooling%20the%20housing%20market%20in%20combination%20with%20interest%20rate%20rises.#:~:text=Reserve%20Bank%20of%20Australia%20assistant%20governor%20Sarah%20Hunter%20has%20said%20risks%20cooling%20the%20housing%20market%20in%20combination%20with%20interest%20rate%20rises.)) warned that the combination of the Budget’s property tax reforms and rising interest rates might risk cooling the housing market. The RBA’s latest forecasts showed dwelling investment would slow to 2% growth by December this year, and fall by 0.3% over 2027.

However, [Treasury’s forecasts](https://www.afr.com/policy/economy/tax-changes-and-rate-rises-risk-cooling-housing-rba-says-20260517-p5zxvw?btis#:~:text=Reserve%20Bank%20of%20Australia%20assistant%20governor%20Sarah%20Hunter%20has%20said%20risks%20cooling%20the%20housing%20market%20in%20combination%20with%20interest%20rate%20rises.#:~:text=Reserve%20Bank%20of%20Australia%20assistant%20governor%20Sarah%20Hunter%20has%20said%20risks%20cooling%20the%20housing%20market%20in%20combination%20with%20interest%20rate%20rises.) were more optimistic, estimating house price growth would be [2% lower](https://www.afr.com/policy/economy/tax-changes-and-rate-rises-risk-cooling-housing-rba-says-20260517-p5zxvw?btis#:~:text=house%20price%20growth%20would%20be%202%20per%20cent%20lower) over the next few years, and rents higher by about $2 a week or $100 a year. The tax changes would [reduce dwelling](https://www.afr.com/policy/economy/tax-changes-and-rate-rises-risk-cooling-housing-rba-says-20260517-p5zxvw?btis#:~:text=reduce%20dwelling%20construction%20by%2035%2C000) construction by 35,000 homes over a decade, although this was projected to be offset by 65,000 additional homes from the Government’s housing supply measures, alongside support for [an additional 75,000 first home buyers](https://www.afr.com/policy/economy/tax-changes-and-rate-rises-risk-cooling-housing-rba-says-20260517-p5zxvw?btis#:~:text=additional%2075%2C000%20first%20buyers).
