## Key issues, provisions and stakeholder comments

### Key Issue 1: CGT changes on non-housing assets and the new 30% tax on capital gains

**Item 5** of Schedule 1 to the Bill outlines a new process for calculating net capital gains. **Item 6 (proposed section 102-6)** controversially extends the CGT changes beyond housing and classifies capital gains, and the underlying assets, into 4 categories ( [Explanatory Memorandum](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/ems/r7493_ems_a90ad43e-17d7-4cd3-859b-84ac4e6f3dea/upload_pdf/JC018386.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf) (EM), pp. 31–35):

- **residential capital gains** (for example, rental property gains arising from 1 July 2027)
- **non-residential capital gains** (for example, gains on commercial property, company shares or interests in a trust arising from 1 July 2027)
- **deferred residential capital gains** (for example, deferred gains from the deemed sale of a rental property on 30 June 2027). (See ‘transitional arrangement’ in Key Issue 2 for discussion of the new Subdivision 112-E ‘deemed sales’).
- **deferred non-residential capital gains** (for example, gains from asset such as commercial property, company shares or interests in a trust deemed disposed of on 30 June 2027 and reacquired on 1 July 2027).

**Item 58**( **proposed Division 119**) of Schedule 1 to the Bill imposes a new minimum 30% tax on individuals for certain capital gains. Key features include:

- it will not apply to recipients of payments prescribed by the Minister via a legislative instrument ( **proposed section 119-15**). The Minister may specify a kind of payment that is a social security payment (such as the Age Pension) or a payment made by an Australian government agency where eligibility for the payment depends on the recipient’s means or financial position or the recipient’s impaired capacity to work or incapacity more broadly (for example income support and pensions for veterans).
- it only applies to capital gains accruing after 1 July 2027, and excludes deferred residential and non-residential gains ( **proposed sections 119-5** to **119-10** of Schedule 1 to the Bill, and **item 1** of the Imposition Bill, **proposed section 12AA** of the Income Tax Rates Act)
- it applies to all CGT assets, except where the asset is a new residential dwelling or affordable housing and the taxpayer opts for CGT discount treatment instead of cost base indexation ( **proposed paragraphs 119-5(2)(b) and (c)**)
- it must be paid on the ‘minimum tax capital gain’ for an income year if the resident individual incurs a ‘minimum tax gap amount’ ( **proposed section 119-10**)
- it may apply to an individual who is a foreigner or temporary resident for part of an income year, but details will be set out in a second tranche of the legislation ( [EM](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/ems/r7493_ems_a90ad43e-17d7-4cd3-859b-84ac4e6f3dea/upload_pdf/JC018386.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf), paragraph 1.178).

As mentioned earlier, the extension of CGT changes to non‑property assets, together with the 30% minimum tax, has been the most contentious aspect of the reforms, attracting opposition from stakeholders, non‑government parties, and most independents.

#### Do the CGT reforms support Australia’s competitiveness and productivity?

The Treasurer [stated](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/transcripts/interview-david-speers-insiders-abc-12#:~:text=We%E2%80%99re%20trying%20to%20remove%20the%20distortion%2C%20David%2C%20by%20applying%20a%20fairer%20and%20more%20neutral%20treatment%20to%20capital%20gains) that extending the reforms to shares and other investments is intended to reduce distortions favouring established housing and promote more neutral capital allocation. The Prime Minister [added](https://www.pm.gov.au/media/australias-economic-outlook-2026#:~:text=And%20investors%20%E2%80%93%20across%20the%20board%20%E2%80%93%20will%20still%20get%20a%20discount%2C%20but%20one%20based%20on%20inflation.#:~:text=And%20investors%20%E2%80%93%20across%20the%20board%20%E2%80%93%20will%20still%20get%20a%20discount%2C%20but%20one%20based%20on%20inflation.) that investors will still get a discount, but one based on inflation, and that the reforms aim to ‘better align the way Australia treats income earned from work, compared to income derived from assets’.

Professor Miranda Stewart [submitted](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=8f15713b-7b8b-468c-a176-ac26bffd4940&subId=793901) that the 50% CGT discount delivered most benefit to the top 10% of taxpayers, and that the CGT reform ‘is a coherent and fair policy choice, that has been demonstrated to work based on Australia’s prior experience with this regime between 1985 and 2000’ (p. 3). She argued that the proposed 30% minimum rate improved fairness for several reasons, with one reason being that:

> the minimum CGT tax rate equalizes the tax rate on capital gains with the 30% rate applicable to companies that hold passive assets, and it applies to assets held in trusts. The 30% rate is also equal to the proposed minimum withholding tax rate on discretionary trust distributions that was announced in the Budget. This ensures greater neutrality in choice of entity for holding investments. There remains a benefit of holding a CGT asset in individual hands as it can benefit from indexation of the cost base, which is not available for companies. (p. 4)

The [Australia Institute](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=3f3362ce-6e92-4c94-af33-278f4d144bab&subId=794177) supported the CGT reforms, arguing that removing the inefficient and distortive 50% discount would improve housing affordability and applying the CGT changes across all assets would avoid introducing new distortions (p. 6). It also contended that the reforms would reduce inequality, and rebalance income tax by reducing tax on labour income and increasing tax on asset income — with younger people being ‘the biggest winners from these changes’ (p. 1).

By contrast, the ACCI [argued](https://acci.com.au/Web/News/Articles/2026/Business-chambers-urge-government-to-scrap-business-tax-hikes.aspx#:~:text=The%20government%E2%80%99s%20stated,competitive%20and%20productive.#:~:text=The%20government%E2%80%99s%20stated,competitive%20and%20productive.) that the measures did not address housing affordability, but penalised investment in small and medium businesses which undermined their productivity and ability to compete. It argued the proposed reform was a ‘tax on productivity’ and comprehensive tax reform was needed to support Australia’s competitiveness and productivity. [Professor Richard Holden](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880773/upload_binary/10880773.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880773%22) also argued that the reform created a ‘Productivity Tax’, which imposed a higher tax rate on businesses with higher productivity than ones with lower productivity (p.1). The [Institute of Public Accountants (IPA)](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880741/upload_binary/10880741.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880741%22) was critical that the reform proposed only ‘piecemeal tax fixes’ while leaving the tax settings that drive productivity untouched.

Media reports indicate that [Treasury was concerned that excluding non-property assets could facilitate avoidance](https://www.afr.com/policy/tax-and-super/investors-dispute-treasury-s-cgt-analysis-20260519-p5zyme?btis#:~:text=Treasury%20concerns%20about,crack%20a%20walnut%E2%80%9D.#:~:text=Treasury%20concerns%20about,crack%20a%20walnut%E2%80%9D.) — for instance, investors could purchase a property through a company and later realise the capital gain through the sale of the company. However, [Pitcher Partners](https://www.afr.com/policy/tax-and-super/investors-dispute-treasury-s-cgt-analysis-20260519-p5zyme#:~:text=Stuart%20Dall%2C%20tax%20partner%20at%20accounting%20firm%20Pitcher%20Partners%2C%20said%20it%20was%20a%20%E2%80%9Csledgehammer%20to%20crack%20a%20walnut%E2%80%9D.#:~:text=Stuart%20Dall%2C%20tax%20partner%20at%20accounting%20firm%20Pitcher%20Partners%2C%20said%20it%20was%20a%20%E2%80%9Csledgehammer%20to%20crack%20a%20walnut%E2%80%9D.) reportedly criticised the Treasury’s response as using a ‘sledgehammer to crack a walnut’.

#### Impact on younger investors

Some younger investors accumulate wealth for a home deposit through [shares or ‘rent‑vesting’](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/transcripts/interview-david-speers-insiders-abc-12#:~:text=we%E2%80%99re%20addressing%20it.-,Speers%3A,Thanks%20David.,-The%20Hon%20Dr) ( [renting](https://www.canstar.com.au/home-loans/rentvesting/#:~:text=Rentvesting%20involves%20renting%20a%20home%20where%20you%20want%20to%20live%2C%20while%20buying%20an%20investment%20property%20in%20an%20area%20you%20can%20afford.#:~:text=Rentvesting%20involves%20renting%20a%20home%20where%20you%20want%20to%20live%2C%20while%20buying%20an%20investment%20property%20in%20an%20area%20you%20can%20afford.) where they live while owning an investment in a more affordable area). While rent-vesting allows [deductions](https://www.canstar.com.au/home-loans/rentvesting/#:~:text=Tax%20benefits,tax%20you%20pay.#:~:text=Tax%20benefits,tax%20you%20pay.) (including interest) and access to negative gearing, disposal of the investment property [attracts CGT](https://www.canstar.com.au/home-loans/rentvesting/#:~:text=rental%20properties%20are%20generally%20subject%20to%20capital%20gains%20tax%20if%20sold%20for%20a%20profit.%20This%20could%20cost%20you%20money%20in%20the%20future%20if%20you%20later%20plan%20to%20upsize%20or%20downsize%20your%20investment.#:~:text=rental%20properties%20are%20generally%20subject%20to%20capital%20gains%20tax%20if%20sold%20for%20a%20profit.%20This%20could%20cost%20you%20money%20in%20the%20future%20if%20you%20later%20plan%20to%20upsize%20or%20downsize%20your%20investment.) if sold at a profit. Under the reforms, these investors may face a higher CGT due to the 30% minimum tax on capital gains.

The Treasurer [advised](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/transcripts/interview-david-speers-insiders-abc-12#:~:text=well%20under%205%C2%A0per%C2%A0cent%20of%20people%20under%2035%20are%20doing%20this.%20They%20can%20continue%20to%20do%20this%20if%20they%20invest%20in%20a%20new%20build%2C%20and%20they%20can%20continue%20to%20do%20it%20if%20they%20already%20own%20that%20home%20before%20Budget%20night.#:~:text=well%20under%205%C2%A0per%C2%A0cent%20of%20people%20under%2035%20are%20doing%20this.%20They%20can%20continue%20to%20do%20this%20if%20they%20invest%20in%20a%20new%20build%2C%20and%20they%20can%20continue%20to%20do%20it%20if%20they%20already%20own%20that%20home%20before%20Budget%20night.) that fewer than 5% of people under 35 use rent-vesting, and that these individuals could continue to invest in new builds, or in established residential properties held prior to Budget night. He further [advised](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/transcripts/interview-david-speers-insiders-abc-12#:~:text=about%209%20in%2010%20people%20under%2035%20don%E2%80%99t%20have%20any%20shares.#:~:text=about%209%20in%2010%20people%20under%2035%20don%E2%80%99t%20have%20any%20shares.) that around 90% of people under 35 do not hold shares; for those who do, the reforms were intended to improve fairness by removing existing tax distortions.

[Devika Shivadekar](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-05-12/budget-2026-share-market-investors-cgt-changes-small-business/106669784#:~:text=Devika%20Shivadekar%2C%20an,outside%20of%20property.%22) (RSM Australia) suggested the changes would likely incentivise alternative wealth-building strategies outside property. However, some [young entrepreneurs](https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/forty-under-40-millennial-entrepreneurs-unite-against-albanese-s-tax-overhaul-20260519-p5zyr6.html) argued that young investors should be exempted from the CGT reforms. As mentioned earlier, independent MP Zali Steggall [called](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Famend%2Fr7493_amend_cf7ae6b2-90ef-410a-a10e-b9d7bf2ce8a4%22) on the Government to ‘consider targeted exemptions or thresholds for modest share investors, so younger Australians are not penalised for using shares and exchange traded funds to build financial security outside the property market’.

#### Impact on small businesses

The PM [said in a speech](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F10882497%22) on Australia’s Economic Outlook 2026 (5 June 2026):

> Around 90 per cent of small business owners will still be eligible for four existing concessions, which remain in place. Meaning if they do decide to sell their business in the future, they will pay less tax or even zero tax on their capital gain.

However, [Business NSW](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880714/upload_binary/10880714.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880714%22) warned that the broader tax reforms (including CGT and trusts) could impose a ‘tax bomb’ on small businesses, discouraging long-term investment and entrepreneurship, and undermining retirement and succession planning.

### Key issue 2: Uncertainty and complexity

CPA Australia [warned](https://www.cpaaustralia.com.au/about-cpa-australia/media/media-releases/tax-reform-conversation-has-a-long-way-to-go#:~:text=CPA%20Australia%20warned,made%20right%20now.%E2%80%9D) that implementing the legislative changes in tranches risked undermining investment confidence, noting investors and taxpayers could not plan financial futures ‘based on half a tax system’ and that it created a two-tier system, where some Australians knew where they stood and others did not. Key [measures creating uncertainty among investors](https://www.cpaaustralia.com.au/about-cpa-australia/media/media-releases/tax-reform-conversation-has-a-long-way-to-go#:~:text=%E2%80%9CThis%20Bill%20is,and%20tax%20consolidation.#:~:text=%E2%80%9CThis%20Bill%20is,and%20tax%20consolidation.) included the proposed [minimum 30% tax on discretionary trusts](https://budget.gov.au/content/factsheets/download/tax-explainers-minimum-tax-discretionary-trusts.pdf), due to be released [later in the year](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/transcripts/interview-sarah-ferguson-730-abc-33#:~:text=Later%20in%20the%20year%20we%E2%80%99ll%20legislate%20the%20trust%20changes.#:~:text=Later%20in%20the%20year%20we%E2%80%99ll%20legislate%20the%20trust%20changes.); the treatment of capital gains for small and start-up businesses; and unclear interactions with managed investment trusts and tax consolidation.

CPA Australia further [argued](https://www.cpaaustralia.com.au/about-cpa-australia/media/media-releases/tax-reform-conversation-has-a-long-way-to-go#:~:text=Ms%20Wong%20said%20the%20reforms,set%20up%2C%E2%80%9D%20Ms%20Wong%20said.#:~:text=Ms%20Wong%20said%20the%20reforms,set%20up%2C%E2%80%9D%20Ms%20Wong%20said.) that the reforms were inconsistent with the Government’s objective of simplifying the tax system, citing multiple new measures and start dates, grandfathering provisions and exemptions, which together made the tax package ‘one of the most complex in recent memory.’

[Thomson Reuters](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe223a5b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0) further commented that while the Bill contained residency tests for indexation and the minimum tax ( **item 24** of Schedule 1 to the Bill, **proposed section 114-25** of the ITAA97), it did not comprehensively deal with residency change issues. The [EM](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/ems/r7493_ems_a90ad43e-17d7-4cd3-859b-84ac4e6f3dea/upload_pdf/JC018386.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf) notes that future amendments may be considered for entities that are resident for only part of an asset's holding period (para 1.63).

#### Negative gearing

From the [2027–28 income year](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe22635b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0), net losses from certain residential dwellings will no longer be deductible against unrelated income (for example, salary, wages or business income). Instead, excess deductions become a ‘quarantined amount’ ( **item 1** of Schedule 2 to the Bill, **proposed paragraph 26-155(1)(b)** of the ITAA97). Any unused amount can generally be carried forward to a later income year ( **proposed paragraph 26-155(1)(c)**). However, carried forward quarantined amounts may be extinguished if the entity becomes bankrupt ( **proposed subsections 26-155(8) and (9)**).

Under **proposed section 26-155** and **proposed subsection 102-5(1)**( **item 5** of Schedule 1), a quarantined amount [may be used](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe22635b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0&comp=wlau&firstPage=true#:~:text=A%20quarantined%20amount%20may%20be%20used%20against%3A) against:

- assessable income from residential dwellings used or held as residential accommodation
- net income from non-quarantined residential dwellings
- gains from revenue assets that are residential dwellings and
- residential capital gains under the amended CGT method statement.

Under **proposed subsections 26-155(2) to (5)**, the quarantining rules [do not apply](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe22635b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0&comp=wlau&firstPage=true#:~:text=The%20quarantining%20rules%20do%20not%20apply%20to%3A) to:

- residential dwellings last acquired before 7:30 pm AEST on 12 May 2026
- new residential dwellings
- dwellings used for activities or purposes determined by the Minister
- dwellings used for businesses or enterprises determined by the Minister
- widely held unit trusts
- complying superannuation entities
- entities in a class determined by the Minister and
- amounts relating to providing fringe benefits.

Both the [CPA](https://www.cpaaustralia.com.au/about-cpa-australia/media/media-releases/tax-reform-conversation-has-a-long-way-to-go#:~:text=CPA%20Australia%20said,term%20financial%20decisions.%E2%80%9D) and the [National Tax and Accountants’ Association](https://www.afr.com/wealth/personal-finance/how-the-new-cgt-rules-work-and-who-faces-higher-taxes-20260527-p601co#:~:text=Likewise%2C%20she%20says%20the%20definition%20of%20%E2%80%9Cnew%20residential%20dwellings%E2%80%9D%20%E2%80%93%20which%20retain%20negative%20gearing%20and%20the%20ability%20to%20choose%20between%20the%20old%20and%20new%20CGT%20discount%20mechanisms%20%E2%80%93%20is%20also%20absent) (NTAA) criticised the absence of a definition of ‘new residential dwelling’ in the Bill. Instead the term will be defined by the Minister by legislative instrument ( **proposed subsections 26-160 (3) and (4)** at **item 1** of Schedule 2). CPA [considered](https://www.cpaaustralia.com.au/about-cpa-australia/media/media-releases/tax-reform-conversation-has-a-long-way-to-go#:~:text=This%20creates%20avoidable%20uncertainty%20at%20a%20time%20when%20Australians%20are%20making%20significant%2C%20long%2Dterm%20financial%20decisions.#:~:text=This%20creates%20avoidable%20uncertainty%20at%20a%20time%20when%20Australians%20are%20making%20significant%2C%20long%2Dterm%20financial%20decisions.) that this ‘creates avoidable uncertainty … for long-term financial decisions.’

#### Transitional arrangement – deemed sales

For assets acquired before 1 July 2027 and realised (for example, sold) on or after that date, the gain [is split](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe223a5b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0&comp=wlau#:~:text=For%20assets%20acquired,the%20new%20rules.#:~:text=For%20assets%20acquired,the%20new%20rules.) into:

- a pre-1 July 2027 component, generally taxed under existing rules and
- a post-1 July 2027 component, taxed under the new rules.

Under **proposed Subdivision 112 ‑ E**, at **item 13** of Schedule 1, assets are **deemed to be disposed of** just before 1 July 2027 and reacquired on that date. The taxpayer does not pay tax on nominal gains resulting from the deemed sale, which are attributable to the period before 1 July 2027, rather, the pre-1 July 2027 component is deferred until realisation.

Under **proposed subsection 112-155(3)** (individuals) or **112-165(3)** (trusts), taxpayers may determine the split using:

- market value at 1 July 2027 or
- a Minister-determined **apportionment method** ( **item 13**, **proposed section 112 ‑ 185**).

The NTAA [expressed concern that](https://www.afr.com/wealth/personal-finance/how-the-new-cgt-rules-work-and-who-faces-higher-taxes-20260527-p601co#:~:text=National%20Tax%20and%20Accountants%E2%80%99%20Association%20senior%20advocate%20Robyn%20Jacobson%20says%20chief%20among%20her%20concerns%20is%20that%20the%20methodology%20for%20apportioning%20gains%20on%20assets%20where%20ownership%20straddles%20the%20old%20and%20new%20CGT%20discount%20systems%20is%20not%20in%20the%20bill.#:~:text=National%20Tax%20and%20Accountants%E2%80%99%20Association%20senior%20advocate%20Robyn%20Jacobson%20says%20chief%20among%20her%20concerns%20is%20that%20the%20methodology%20for%20apportioning%20gains%20on%20assets%20where%20ownership%20straddles%20the%20old%20and%20new%20CGT%20discount%20systems%20is%20not%20in%20the%20bill.) prescribing the apportionment method by legislative instrument reduces parliamentary scrutiny. Corrs Chambers Westgarth [similarly noted that the apportionment method could be amended or replaced by successive Ministers](https://www.corrs.com.au/insights/capital-gains-tax-and-negative-gearing-amendments-key-changes-and-implications#:~:text=By%20delegating%20the%20detail%20of%20key%20aspects%20of%20the%20CGT%20and%20negative%20gearing%20changes%20in%20this%20way%2C%20there%20is%20a%20risk%20of%20replacement%20or%20amendment%20of%20the%20method%20by%20successive%20Ministers.%C2%A0), and that [the lack of detail](https://www.corrs.com.au/insights/capital-gains-tax-and-negative-gearing-amendments-key-changes-and-implications#:~:text=a%20later%20date.-,This%20lack%20of%20detail,-should%20be%20resolved) of the method created uncertainty, as it may influence taxpayer behaviour ahead of 1 July 2027. Absent clarity, taxpayers may need to rely on **market valuations**, increasing compliance costs.

### Key issue 3: Replacement of the 50% CGT discount with cost base indexation

For [eligible CGT assets held for at least 12 months](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe223a5b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0), the existing 50% CGT discount will generally be replaced by **cost base indexation** for gains accruing from 1 July 2027 ( **items 2, 8 to 11, 14 to 22, and 48–50** of Schedule 1 to the Bill). Indexation adjusts the cost base by reference to CPI so that only real gains are taxed. The new indexation regime applies to:

- Australian resident individuals
- trusts, broadly to the extent gains flow to eligible Australian resident individuals and
- individuals in respect of partnership gains.

The [50% CGT discount](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe223a5b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0&comp=wlau#:~:text=The%2050%25%20CGT%20discount%20will,not%20affected%20by%20the%20reforms.#:~:text=The%2050%25%20CGT%20discount%20will,not%20affected%20by%20the%20reforms.) will generally continue to apply to:

- capital gains accrued before 1 July 2027
- eligible new residential dwellings, where the taxpayer opts for the discount instead of indexation
- eligible affordable housing, where the existing higher discount is retained, and
- certain entities or assets outside the reforms.

Companies, complying superannuation entities, life insurance companies, foreign residents and temporary residents are generally [excluded from](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe223a5b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&VR=3.0&RS=cblt1.0&comp=wlau#:~:text=Exemptions,new%20indexation%20regime.#:~:text=Exemptions,new%20indexation%20regime.) the new indexation regime.

Treasury estimates suggest only a modest increase in the average tax rate on capital gains (from [19.3% to 21.4%](https://www.afr.com/policy/tax-and-super/chalmers-answers-cgt-outcry-average-rate-to-rise-just-2pc-20260518-p5zyhl)) over the next decade, with limited expected impact on overall investment in the economy. The [e61 Institute](https://newshub.medianet.com.au/2026/05/indexing-capital-gains-makes-tax-system-fairer-e61/152811/#:~:text=e61%20has%20consistently%20argued%20that%20inflation%20indexation%20is%20the%20right%20solution%20to%20CGT%20reform) supported cost base indexation, arguing that it improved fairness compared to the CGT discount method.

[Professor David Stern](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=611b790d-6c26-433c-9a42-49e2c7791f6d&subId=792419) and [Allan Gray Australia](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=4cf47cb8-c09d-4e9f-ab22-7c2050487bf7&subId=793736) argued that the CGT discount remained preferable for business assets because the CGT discount helped better align the tax treatment of reinvested earnings and dividends, whereas indexation alone did not. They argued that the indexation method would encourage companies to pay out earnings in the form of franked dividends, rather than reinvest profits into the business.

The [Financial Services Council (FSC)](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/media/pressrel/10880732/upload_binary/10880732.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf#search=%22media/pressrel/10880732%22) said the CGT reforms ‘could materially increase taxes on Australians investing outside superannuation, including younger Australians, families, part-time workers and Australians approaching retirement’. [Westbridge Funds Management](https://www.aph.gov.au/DocumentStore.ashx?id=09d41158-3904-46d3-86b2-35d3acdc28a5&subId=793319) submitted that restricting negative gearing for established residential property was likely to reduce investor participation and place upward pressure on rents; and replacing the 50% CGT discount with indexation would materially reduce the reward for higher risk (p. 4).

## Schedule 3: Working Australians Tax Offset

### Background

The Working Australians Tax Offset (WATO) was announced in the Budget as a [non-refundable tax offset](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/tax-offsets/about-tax-offsets#:~:text=A%20tax%20offset,tax%20below%20zero.#:~:text=A%20tax%20offset,tax%20below%20zero.) of up to $250 a year for individuals earning labour income from 1 July 2027 ([Budget Paper No. 2](https://budget.gov.au/content/bp2/download/bp2_2026-27.pdf) (pp. 16–17)). WATO is estimated to benefit [over 13 million workers](https://budget.gov.au/content/factsheets/download/tax-explainers-new-tax-cuts-workers.pdf) (p. 1). This measure is non-controversial and has received wide support.

### Key provisions

Schedule 3 to the Bill introduces the WATO from 1 July 2027. Under **proposed section 61-155** of the ITAA97, at **item 1** of Schedule 3 to the Bill, an individual is eligible if:

- they are an Australian resident at any time during the income year and
- their net labour income exceeds the tax-free threshold.

Under **proposed section 61-160**, the amount of the offset is the lesser of $250 and an amount determined by the Minister via legislative instrument.

[Thomson Reuters](https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/Document/I47fe22335b2911f184d0de003bc213a9/View/FullText.html?navigationPath=Search%2Fv1%2Fresults%2Fnavigation%2Fi0a93d3a50000019ea9fbb8486fd750b5%3Fppcid%3D8bbe71c558a74166a9cf869567f186f7%26Nav%3DAUNZ_CURRENT_AWARENESS%26fragmentIdentifier%3DI47fe22335b2911f184d0de003bc213a9%26parentRank%3D0%26startIndex%3D1%26contextData%3D%2528sc.Search%2529%26transitionType%3DSearchItem&listSource=Search&listPageSource=171788ad269a6f23eb33958d98babded&list=AUNZ_CURRENT_AWARENESS&rank=5&sessionScopeId=fa317c515a8588edc0d0953725f747b982521f28a045032b88efd39349d1d095&ppcid=8bbe71c558a74166a9cf869567f186f7&originationContext=Search%20Result&transitionType=SearchItem&contextData=(sc.Search)&comp=wlau#:~:text=The%20Bill%20has%20a%20narrower%20operation) noted that the Bill has a narrower operation than the Budget announcement as it requires Australian residency, net labour income above the tax-free threshold, and the offset is non-refundable. Accordingly, a worker with labour income below the tax-free threshold, or with insufficient tax payable, may not receive the full $250 benefit and may receive no practical benefit.

## Schedule 4: Standard deduction for work-related expenses

### Background and policy development

The idea of implementing a standard deduction without receipts for most taxpayers was proposed in the [Henry Review](https://treasury.gov.au/review/the-australias-future-tax-system-review/final-report) ( [Part 1](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2019-10/afts_final_report_part_1_consolidated.pdf), p. 31). In April 2025, during the federal election campaign, the Government [announced](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22media%2Fpressrel%2F10257274%22) the $1,000 instant tax deduction as an alternative to claiming work‑related expenses, from 1 July 2026. The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) [released a costing estimate](https://www.pbo.gov.au/elections/2025-general-election/2025-election-commitments-costings/1000-instant-tax-deduction-work-related-expenses) for the measure. In April-May 2026, Treasury [consulted](https://aus01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fconsult.treasury.gov.au%2Fc2026-757530&data=05%7C02%7Celo.guo-hawkins%40aph.gov.au%7C6bba43a61ff649fd91b208dea1c73188%7Cf6214c153a9947d1b862c9648e927316%7C0%7C0%7C639126074739181393%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=V8KO9hnxCqMPZqGDADYMIRQN9Ob9lzham6%2FwJnkPLbM%3D&reserved=0) on [draft](https://storage.googleapis.com/files-au-treasury/treasury/p/prj3bfb4b9344392ae4d553b/page/c2026_757530_ed.pdf) legislation; at the time of writing, submissions have not been published on the Treasury website.

The 2026–27 Budget [confirmed](https://budget.gov.au/content/bp2/download/bp2_2026-27.pdf) the measure (p. 19), with an [estimated](https://ministers.treasury.gov.au/ministers/jim-chalmers-2022/media-releases/1000-instant-tax-deduction-deliver-lower-simpler-taxes) **6.2 million workers** ( **42% of taxpayers**) benefiting, with an average **saving of $205.**

### What does Schedule 4 do?

Schedule 4 to the Bill will amend tax laws to:

- introduce a standard deduction of **up to $1,000** for Australian tax residents who earn ‘labour income’ (for example, including salary, wages, bonuses; excluding personal service income) under certain PAYG withholding provisions, **starting 1 July 2026**
- the maximum amount of $1,000 applies to deductions for _work-related expenses_ that are incurred in producing labour income
- keep current arrangements, including requiring full substantiation of each expense, for taxpayers who:
  - have more than $1,000 in work-related expenses or
  - earn income only from business, investment or self-employment activities.
- allow deductions for certain _other expenses_ to be claimed in addition to the standard tax deduction
- update substantiation and capital allowance rules to support the new standard deduction
- repeal the existing no-receipt threshold of $300 for all deductions and $150 specifically for laundry expenses.

The optional $1,000 standard deduction is **not a full $1,000 tax refund**. It is a $1,000 reduction that reduces one’s taxable income. For instance, if someone pays a 30% marginal tax rate, this deduction reduces their tax bill by $300 ($1,000 x 0.30).

### Overview of the current work-related tax deductions

Deductible expenses are either work-related expenses, or other expenses. Work-related deductions reduce taxable income and must meet the ATO’s ‘ [3 golden rules](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/guides-for-occupations-and-industries/occupation-and-industry-specific-guides#:~:text=To%20claim%20a,usually%20a%20receipt).#:~:text=To%20claim%20a,usually%20a%20receipt).)’:

1. The taxpayer must have spent the money, and not received reimbursement.
2. The expense must directly relate to earning the taxpayer’s income.
3. The taxpayer must [keep records](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/records-you-need-to-keep) (for example, a receipt) to show that they incurred the expense.

In the 2022–23 income year (data released on 27 June 2025), the ATO reported that the average work-related expenses claimed was [$2,739](https://www.ato.gov.au/media-centre/2022-23-taxation-statistics-released#:~:text=an%20average%20of%20%242%2C739%C2%A0per%20person.#:~:text=an%20average%20of%20%242%2C739%C2%A0per%20person.), which is significantly higher than the $1,000 proposed. Examples of existing [work-related expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions), typically claimed by taxpayers include:

- [cars, transport and travel](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/cars-transport-and-travel)
- [tools, computers, mobiles, internet, stationery and other items used for work](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/tools-computers-and-items-you-use-for-work)
- [occupation-specific clothing and protective equipment](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/clothes-and-items-you-wear-at-work)
- [work from home expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/working-from-home-expenses)
- [self-education, seminars, conferences and training](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/education-training-and-seminars)
- [compulsory medical assessments required by employers and COVID-19 tests](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/work-related-deductions/personal-grooming-health-and-fitness/medical-and-dental-expenses-vaccinations-and-covid-19-tests).

Examples of [other expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/how-to-claim-deductions#:~:text=tax%20return%20easier.-,Other%20expenses%20you%20can%20claim,-There%20are%20a), which are not work-related, include:

- [gifts and donations](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/gifts-and-donations)
- [union fees, professional memberships, working with children check, agency fees and commissions](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/memberships-accreditations-fees-and-commissions)
- expenses related to earning income from [investments](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/investments-insurance-and-super)
- [personal super contributions and income protection insurance](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/investments-insurance-and-super)
- the [cost of managing tax affairs](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/cost-of-managing-tax-affairs).

Currently there is a $300 standard deduction that a taxpayer may claim, without receipts, if the total of all their work expenses (including laundry expenses) is $300 or less: [subsection 900-35(1)](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s900.35.html#:~:text=(1),keeping%20travel%20records.#:~:text=(1),keeping%20travel%20records.) of the ITAA97. If the total is more than $300, the taxpayer needs to substantiate _all_ the work expenses, not just the excess over $300. There is also an instant deduction of $150, without receipts, for laundry expenses: [section 900-40](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s900.40.html) of the ITAA97.

## Key issues and provisions

**Items 1** and **3** of Schedule 1 to the Bill introduce a new maximum $1,000 standard deduction for work-related expenses. **Proposed section 25-130** in **item 3** sets eligibility, limiting access to Australian _workers_ with ‘ **assessable labour income**’ only. **Proposed subsection** **25-130(4)** defines _assessable labour income_ by reference to PAYG (Pay As You Go) withholding provisions in Schedule 1 to the [Taxation Administration Act 1953](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C1953A00001/latest/text)(TAA), covering:

- payments for work and services (for example, payments to employees, directors, office holders and religious practitioners, and return-to-work payments) (sections 12-35 to 12-50 in Subdivision 12-B)
- payments on retirement or termination of employment (Subdivision 12-C)
- parental leave pay (paragraph 12-110(1)(ca)).

Individuals who are ineligible for the standard deductions because they do not derive assessable labour income, [include](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/hiring-and-paying-your-workers/payg-withholding/payments-you-need-to-withhold-from):

- independent contractors (in general)
- sole traders
- partners in partnerships.

The maximum benefit the standard deduction will yield [is expected to be $470](https://www.austaxpolicy.com/budget-forum-2026-whats-hiding-within-the-proposed-1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=The%20maximum%20benefit%20the%20standard%20deduction%20will%20yield%20is%20expected%20to%20be%20%24470%2C%20falling%20to%20the%20highest%20income%20earners.#:~:text=The%20maximum%20benefit%20the%20standard%20deduction%20will%20yield%20is%20expected%20to%20be%20%24470%2C%20falling%20to%20the%20highest%20income%20earners.) for the highest income earners. This deduction [cannot add to or create a loss](https://www.austaxpolicy.com/budget-forum-2026-whats-hiding-within-the-proposed-1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=this%20deduction%20cannot%20add%20to%20or%20create%20a%20loss%20%E2%80%93%20it%20is%20limited%20to%20the%20extent%20of%20labour%20income%20(proposed%20in%20subsection%2025%2D130(2)%20ITAA97).#:~:text=this%20deduction%20cannot%20add%20to%20or%20create%20a%20loss%20%E2%80%93%20it%20is%20limited%20to%20the%20extent%20of%20labour%20income%20(proposed%20in%20subsection%2025%2D130(2)%20ITAA97).) – it is limited to the extent of labour income: **proposed subsection 25-130(2) ITAA97**.

### Deductions that can be claimed in addition to the standard deduction

Some deductions under **proposed subsection 25-130(3)** can be claimed separately to, and independent of, the standard deduction, for example, insurance premiums for income protection, and membership fees of a trade, business or professional association.

Other deductions that can be claimed in addition to the standard deduction include: deductions unconnected with labour income (for example, interest income deductions); and specific deductions such as for gifts and costs of managing tax affairs.

### Key issue: Complexity and unintended consequences

Submitters to the consultation on the draft legislation (including [Chartered Accountants ANZ, CPA Australia, The Tax Institute](https://www.charteredaccountantsanz.com/news-and-analysis/advocacy/policy-submissions/joint-submission-calls-for-refinement-to-$1000-standard-tax-deduction) (the Joint Bodies), [Etax Accountants](https://www.etax.com.au/1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=Why%20Are%20They,smaller%20tax%20refunds.#:~:text=Why%20Are%20They,smaller%20tax%20refunds.), [National Tax & Accountants’ Association](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22library%2Fjrnart%2F10869841%22) (NTAA) and [National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22library%2Fjrnart%2F10869795%22) (NALSPA)) supported the policy intent of red tape reduction but raised concerns about unintended consequences and equity concerns. (Schedule 4 of the Bill is identical to the exposure draft legislation).

The [Tax and Transfer Policy Institute](https://www.austaxpolicy.com/budget-forum-2026-whats-hiding-within-the-proposed-1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=The%20draft%20legislation%20is%20quite%20lengthy.%20It%20adds%20inherent%20complexity%20to%20the%20tax%20legislation%20by%20virtue%20of%20flow%20on%20amendments%20to%20substantiation%2C%20capital%20allowances%20rules%20and%20fringe%20benefits%20regime.#:~:text=The%20draft%20legislation%20is%20quite%20lengthy.%20It%20adds%20inherent%20complexity%20to%20the%20tax%20legislation%20by%20virtue%20of%20flow%20on%20amendments%20to%20substantiation%2C%20capital%20allowances%20rules%20and%20fringe%20benefits%20regime.) (TTPI) submitted that the draft legislation risked distorting the income tax system by creating a [two-tiered system](https://www.austaxpolicy.com/budget-forum-2026-whats-hiding-within-the-proposed-1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=The%20distortion%20in,the%20tax%20system%3F) where one cohort of taxpayers received a deduction without incurring any loss or outgoing, and another cohort, those with genuine work-related expenses, faced higher compliance obligations than under the existing law: ‘This raises [an issue of horizontal equity](https://www.austaxpolicy.com/budget-forum-2026-whats-hiding-within-the-proposed-1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=This%20raises%20questions%20of%20horizontal%20equity%2C%20as%20compliant%20taxpayers%20with%20real%20outlays%20may%20be%20worse%20off.%20Firstly%2C%20in%20terms%20of%20the%20compliance%20burden%2C%20and%2C%20secondly%2C%20if%20they%20opt%20to%20swap%20to%20the%20standard%20deduction%20due%20to%20the%20compliance%20burden%2C%20they%20may%20also%20be%20financially%20disadvantaged.#:~:text=This%20raises%20questions%20of%20horizontal%20equity%2C%20as%20compliant%20taxpayers%20with%20real%20outlays%20may%20be%20worse%20off.%20Firstly%2C%20in%20terms%20of%20the%20compliance%20burden%2C%20and%2C%20secondly%2C%20if%20they%20opt%20to%20swap%20to%20the%20standard%20deduction%20due%20to%20the%20compliance%20burden%2C%20they%20may%20also%20be%20financially%20disadvantaged.).’

#### Potential contravention of non-discrimination articles in double tax agreements

The TTPI raised the [potential issue](https://www.austaxpolicy.com/budget-forum-2026-whats-hiding-within-the-proposed-1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=There%20are%20further,on%20this%20point.#:~:text=There%20are%20further,on%20this%20point.) that making the standard deduction unavailable to non‑residents and temporary residents may potentially conflict with the High Court of Australia’s 2021 decision in [Addy v Commissioner of Taxation](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/cases/cth/HCA/2021/34.html).

#### Taxpayers may receive smaller tax refunds than their legitimate entitlements when using standard deductions

Stakeholders (including [Etax Accountants](https://www.etax.com.au/1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=Why%20Are%20They,smaller%20tax%20refunds.#:~:text=Why%20Are%20They,smaller%20tax%20refunds.), [CPA Australia](https://www.cpaaustralia.com.au/about-cpa-australia/media/media-releases/cpa-australia-responds-to-alp-instant-tax-deduction-pledge), the [Joint Bodies](https://www.charteredaccountantsanz.com/news-and-analysis/advocacy/policy-submissions/joint-submission-calls-for-refinement-to-$1000-standard-tax-deduction) and the [Institute of Public Accountants](https://www.accountantsdaily.com.au/tax-compliance/21186-labors-standard-deduction-may-expose-taxpayers-to-future-tax-consequences) (IPA)) noted that the standard deduction does not increase overall deduction generosity. [Etax Accountants](https://www.etax.com.au/1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=Why%20Are%20They,smaller%20tax%20refunds.#:~:text=Why%20Are%20They,smaller%20tax%20refunds.) reported the [average taxpayer claims around $3,000 in deductions](https://www.etax.com.au/1000-instant-tax-deduction/#:~:text=We%20should%20also%20remember%20that%20the%20average%20total%20deduction%20claimed%20by%20an%20Australian%20taxpayer%20is%20around%20%243000); opting for a $1,000 standard deduction may therefore reduce refunds despite legitimate entitlements. While convenient, the measure risked discouraging taxpayers from claiming their full entitlements.
